what_its_for: Dexmedetomidine is used to help you feel calm and relaxed. It is used in two main ways: (1) In the hospital or ICU, it is given through an IV to sedate patients on a breathing machine or during medical procedures. (2) The under-the-tongue (sublingual) film version (Igalmi) is used to calm agitation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder when feelings of restlessness or agitation come on suddenly.
how_to_take: This medicine is given by a healthcare provider — never at home on your own. The IV form is given directly into your vein by a nurse in a hospital setting. The sublingual film (Igalmi) is placed under your tongue or between your cheek and gum by a healthcare provider. You must let the film dissolve completely — do not chew, swallow, or move it around. Do not eat or drink anything until the film has fully dissolved. Stay seated or lying down during and after receiving this medicine because it can cause dizziness or low blood pressure.
dosing: Your doctor and care team will decide the exact dose based on your age, weight, medical condition, and how you respond to the medicine. For the IV form used in the ICU, doses are carefully adjusted throughout the day by your nurses and doctors. For the sublingual film (Igalmi), a common starting dose for adults is 120 mcg or 180 mcg placed under the tongue, and a second dose may be given by your provider after 2 hours if needed. Never try to adjust or give yourself this medicine on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is always given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting, you will not need to worry about missing a dose on your own. Your care team will manage all dosing. If you have concerns about your treatment schedule, speak with your doctor or nurse.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled entirely by healthcare professionals. If you have been given any supplies to take home (which is very rare), keep them in a cool, dry place away from heat, moisture, and light. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use any medicine that looks discolored or has particles floating in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol and other sedating substances before and after receiving this medicine, as they can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or make important decisions for at least 24 hours after receiving this medicine, as it can slow your thinking and reaction time. Avoid getting up too quickly after receiving the sublingual film, as this can cause dizziness and falls. Tell your care team about all other medicines, supplements, and herbal products you take, especially sleep aids, anxiety medicines, blood pressure medicines, or pain medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor or go to an emergency room right away if you experience: very slow or shallow breathing, heart beating very slowly or irregularly, sudden drop in blood pressure (feeling faint, lightheaded, or passing out), unusual weakness, confusion that gets worse, or any allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. After leaving the hospital or clinic, call your doctor if you feel your heart is beating oddly, you feel extremely dizzy, or your agitation does not improve.
when_it_works: This medicine works very quickly. When given through an IV, you may start feeling calm and sleepy within minutes. The sublingual film for agitation typically begins to work within 20 to 30 minutes of placing it under your tongue. The calming effects of the sublingual film can last several hours. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely the entire time this medicine is working.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): Lower doses may be used because older adults are more sensitive to this medicine and have a higher risk of low blood pressure and slow heart rate. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor may adjust your dose if your kidneys or liver are not working well, since these organs help remove the medicine from your body. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this medicine during pregnancy and breastfeeding is not fully known, and your doctor will carefully weigh the risks and benefits. Children: The IV form is sometimes used in children in hospital settings, but only under close medical supervision with specially adjusted doses. The sublingual film is currently approved only for adults 18 and older.
